clue.text: Like the best part of choice jelly

parts.note: as means like, in the sense of in the manner of

indicators.note: the best part of a word is most of it, so its final letter is dropped here

parts.note: a pick is a choice, as in take your pick

explanation.surface: Someone praising the finest portion of a selected jelly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'best part of' trims PICK to PIC; AS comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspic is a savoury gelatine made from meat stock, used to glaze or set cold dishes.

clue.text: Taking into custody for striking

definitions.meaning: what police do when detaining a suspect

explanation.surface: Police make an arrest over a strike.
explanation.definitionFit: Arresting means both detaining by law and catching the attention.

clue.text: Steam trains available for smokers

definitions.meaning: puffer is a childish name for a steam engine

explanation.surface: Old locomotives offered to cigarette users.
explanation.definitionFit: Puffer is both nursery slang for a locomotive and someone who puffs on a pipe.

clue.text: Excellent attempt to solve

definitions.meaning: a try, as in have a ... at it
to work out, as in break a code

explanation.surface: A fine try at solving a puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Crack means first-rate, a go at something, and to break or decipher.

clue.text: Make an inventory, as shoplifters do

definitions.meaning: to count up the goods held in a shop or store
read literally, thieves in a shop help themselves to its merchandise

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper counts goods while thieves carry them off.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking stock is the phrase for a formal stock count; literally, shoplifters walk off with goods.

clue.text: Poorer but solvent

definitions.meaning: a liquid such as turps used to dilute paint

explanation.surface: Someone with less money who still pays their debts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'solvent' looks financial beside 'Poorer', but means a paint diluent.
explanation.definitionFit: Thinner is the comparative of thin, sparser, and a noun for a paint-diluting liquid.

clue.text: Sort of energy making cattle twitch

parts.note: kine is an old plural of cow, meaning cattle
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: Livestock jumping about as if electrified.
explanation.definitionFit: Kinetic energy is the energy a body has from its motion.

clue.text: Gamble' recklessly — but don't start to embezzle

annotationWithheld.why: Gamble recklessly - but don't start to embezzle: the answer minus its first letter gives PECULATE (embezzle); nothing in the clue supplies S, and the grammar has no form for this subtractive definition
annotationWithheld.clue: Gamble' recklessly — but don't start to embezzle

clue.text: Top clue reworked many times

indicators.note: reworked says the letters of top clue are put into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A setter revises a leading clue over and over.
explanation.definitionFit: Octuple means eightfold, multiplied a number of times.

clue.text: Book-end, a present, is broken

parts.note: the end of the word book is K
to put a case is to present it

explanation.surface: A gift of a bookend arrives smashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book-end' looks like the shelf support but means the last letter of Book.
explanation.definitionFit: Kaput is slang, from German, for broken or finished.

clue.text: Spending more money on accommodation one takes on

parts.note: re means on or concerning, as in a letter heading
a flat is a piece of accommodation
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone splashing out on lodgings and the lodger they take in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes' is a link word; the second 'on' is the final ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Reflation is economic policy that boosts spending and the money supply to lift a sluggish economy.

clue.text: Last of the tankards returned to bar

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, here of the word the
returned says the word for tankards is read backwards

parts.note: pots are drinking vessels such as tankards

explanation.surface: The final tankards are brought back to the pub bar.
explanation.walkthrough: E, then 'returned' turns POTS into STOP.
explanation.definitionFit: Estop is a legal term meaning to bar or preclude someone from asserting something.

clue.text: Aid for listener, achieving best advantage in radio

indicators.note: in tells us the two words for achieving best and advantage sit inside the word for radio

parts.note: a radio is a wireless set
peaking means reaching one's highest point
a trump is a winning card, an advantage held in reserve

explanation.surface: A gadget that helps you hear, praised as being at its best on the wireless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' splits the radio word around the rest; 'achieving best' is reaching a peak, not winning.
explanation.definitionFit: A speaking trumpet is a horn-shaped device that carries the voice, also once held to the ear by the hard of hearing.

clue.text: Like parish pump, surrounded by water

definitions.meaning: parish-pump means narrowly local in outlook
the sense of an island, girt by sea

explanation.surface: A village pump on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: Parish-pump politics is a British idiom for petty local concerns.
explanation.definitionFit: Insular means both narrow-minded and of an island; parish-pump is parochial.

clue.text: Power — unless it's turned off

indicators.note: turned off suggests the letters of unless it's are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: A device's power fails unless it has been switched off.
explanation.definitionFit: Lustiness is vigour or robust strength.

clue.text: Drink served twice at upper-class country house

parts.note: cha is a slang word for tea
tea itself, the same drink a second time
U is the abbreviation for upper-class, as opposed to non-U

explanation.surface: Tea poured twice over for the gentry at a country seat.
explanation.walkthrough: CHA and TEA are the same drink under two names; U as upper-class comes from 1950s British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A chateau is a French castle or large country residence.

clue.text: Playing badly, as usual — MC in disarray

indicators.note: disarray means a muddle, so the letters before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: The band plays poorly as ever, with the compere all at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' is a link and 'in' is fodder: USUAL MC IN rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Unmusical means lacking melody or skill in music.

clue.text: Broom providing seating when subjected to new spell

indicators.note: being given a new spelling means the letters of seating are rearranged

explanation.surface: A broom cupboard offers seats once a witch casts a fresh spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when subjected to' is linking; 'new spell' is a pun on spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Genista is a genus of shrubs including the broom family.

clue.text: Nothing to do with the hearing of East African people

parts.note: nil means nothing or zero
otic means relating to the ear

explanation.surface: An ethnographer finds no link with the hearing of a people in East Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Nilotic describes peoples of the Nile region, such as the Dinka and Maasai.

clue.text: A way to explore the unknown

definitions.text: A way to explore the unknown

parts.words: A way to explore the unknown
parts.note: reads like an expedition, but the unknown is the mathematician's x

explanation.surface: An adventurer's method for charting uncharted lands.
explanation.definitionFit: This branch of mathematics uses symbols to solve for unknown quantities.

clue.text: Mineral found in the mine's entrance? Prove it!

indicators.note: found in says the mineral word is placed inside the following letters
the entrance of a word is its first letter, here of mine's

parts.note: ore is mineral-bearing rock

explanation.surface: A miner finds rock at the pit entrance and is challenged to demonstrate it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' places the mineral inside. The definition is cheeky: a theorem is a statement waiting to be proved.
explanation.definitionFit: A theorem is a mathematical statement that must be demonstrated by proof.

clue.text: Vehicle no sane person would get off?

definitions.text: Vehicle no sane person would get off?

parts.words: Vehicle no sane person would get off?
parts.note: a play on the British idiom off one's rocker or cart, meaning crazy, applied to a cart that sane people stay on

explanation.surface: A cart that only lunatics would step down from.
explanation.walkthrough: To be 'off your trolley' is British slang for being mad.
explanation.definitionFit: A trolley is a wheeled cart, and being off it means losing one's sanity.

clue.text: Duck included in list, or another fowl

indicators.note: included in says the duck letter goes inside the list word

parts.note: a roster is a list of duties or names
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, O

explanation.surface: A duck appears on a poultry list along with another bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like the bird, setting up 'another fowl'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rooster is a cockerel, the male domestic chicken.

clue.text: Capital profits originated by Duke

definitions.note: the definition is a descriptive phrase rather than a noun

parts.note: Wellington is the capital of New Zealand
boot is an old word for profit or advantage

explanation.surface: Gains in the capital started by a nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: The boots are named after the Duke of Wellington, who popularised them; 'boots' as profits is archaic, as in 'to boot'.
explanation.definitionFit: The rubber footwear is named after the first Duke of Wellington, who made the style fashionable.

clue.text: Old councillors making humorous remarks over a name

parts.note: wit is clever humour or funny remarks

explanation.surface: Elderly council members cracking jokes about someone's name.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts WIT above AN.
explanation.definitionFit: The witan was the Anglo-Saxon king's council of wise men.

clue.text: Balloon's source of ballast exhausted

indicators.note: the source of a word is its opening letter, here of ballast

parts.note: limp means drooping or tired out

explanation.surface: A balloon sags once its sandbags run out.
explanation.definitionFit: A blimp is a non-rigid airship or barrage balloon.

clue.text: Contribution may be only a little but it helps

indicators.note: only a little says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A small donation still does some good.
explanation.definitionFit: A tithe is a tenth of income given to the church, a kind of contribution.

clue.text: How like a missile -first sign of landing is in the sea

indicators.note: in places these letters inside the name of the sea

parts.note: the Baltic is a sea of northern Europe

indicators.note: the first sign of a word is its opening letter, here of landing

explanation.surface: A missile comes down in the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' places the landing letter and 'is' inside the sea's name; 'How like a missile' is read as 'in the manner of a missile'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballistic describes the path of a projectile flying under gravity, as a missile does.

clue.text: Translation of Seneca's lines required

indicators.note: a translation renders a text anew, so the letters of the Roman's name are reordered

parts.note: RY is short for railway, lines of track

explanation.surface: A rendering of the Roman philosopher's verse is set for study.
explanation.walkthrough: Seneca's gives SENECAS, shuffled to NECESSA.
explanation.definitionFit: Necessary means needed or required.

clue.text: Exposure to risk for each one left

parts.note: per means for each, as in per head
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Each person still standing is in danger.
explanation.definitionFit: Peril means danger, the state of being exposed to harm.
